newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels seek talks but give envoys nothing.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels seek talks but give envoys nothing.

text.p: Peru's hostage crisis dragged into its 19th day on Sunday with Marxist rebels who are holding 74 captives calling for talks but giving nothing tangible to church and Red Cross envoys who visited the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.
A Japanese newspaper said the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels were demanding up to $30 million in ransom from Japanese firms whose executives they hold.

But Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Sunday he was not aware of any ransom demands and that the government had not been approached. The Mainichi Shimbun, quoting "informed sources", said the MRTA had demanded the money as a "war tax".

The MRTA call for talks -- daubed on a banner that the rebels unfurled on the roof of the complex early on Saturday -- were answered by a visit from Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani and Red Cross mediator Michel Minnig later in the day.
It was the first time that Cipriani, a close friend of President Alberto Fujimori, had been to the residence since Wednesday when the last seven hostages were released.
The two men spent two hours inside but left empty handed and did not speak to the crowds of jounalists still camped out in the streets surrounding the compound.
Pope John Paul, in an apparent appeal to Marxist guerrillas holding 74 hostages in Peru, on Sunday urged kidnappers and hostage-takers to free their captives as a "gesture of humanity."
"The mercy of Christ, born of human weakness, urges hostage-takers to fulfil this gesture of humanity -- free these people," the pope told pilgrims in St Peter's Square at his regular Sunday address.
He made no direct reference to the Peru crisis but said his thoughts and prayers were with families missing loved ones over the Christmas period.
In the long periods while Cipriani and government negotiator Domingo Palermo have stayed away from the residence, the Red Cross has acted as the only contact between the rebels and the outside world.
"We are maintaining our offer of being an intermediary of information," Red Cross spokesman Ronald Bigler told Reuters.
But Bigler added that the Red Cross could only be of limited help in reaching agreement over the main sticking points in the standoff.
"Eventually it must come to face-to-face talks," he said.
The rebel banners, three in all, included the messages: "Nobody in here is giving up" and "Mr Fujimori, with arrogant declarations and without dialogue, there will never be a solution."

In a hard-hitting speech Thursday, Fujimori had rejected the rebels' claim to be fighting for Peru's poor and condemned them as "terrorists" bent on violence. He has ruled out their main demand that about 400 jailed MRTA comrades be pardoned.
The increasingly bitter war of words replaced signs of conciliation and dialogue before the new year.
Face-to-face talks between Palermo and the rebels on Dec. 28 secured the freedom of 20 hostages, but he has not met them since and a sporadic dribble of releases has dried up in recent days.

Hashimoto nevertheless planned to leave Tokyo on Tuesday and go ahead with a five-day trip to Asian nations, saying this was a sign of his confidence in the Peruvian government's ability to handle the situation.
The stand-off began on Dec. 17 when about 20 MRTA rebels burst in to a cocktail party at the residence being held in honour of Japanese Emperor Akihito.

The rebels inside the building underlined their defiant stand by hoisting their red and white flag alongside the propaganda banners unfurled Saturday, emblazoned with a mace and rifle and the image of Tupac Amaru -- an 18th-century Andean Indian who led a bloody uprising against Spanish colonial rule.

The guerrillas have mined and booby trapped the residence against possible attack and warned that any attempt to take the building by force would lead to many deaths. No hostages have been killed or injured in the standoff and freed men have said they were treated well by the rebels.
The remaining captives included Fujimori's brother, two ambassadors, top Peruvian government officials and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
